excerpt: MaxLinear raises its 2026 optical revenue outlook to $250-$270 million as AI demand surges, with 1.6T products and hyperscaler orders fueling growth prospects.
headline: MXL Q3 Earnings Call Highlights AI Growth and Optical Demand
html_content:
MaxLinear, Inc. MXL highlighted accelerating AI data center demand, expanding optical connectivity opportunities and improving profitability during its third-quarter 2026 earnings call. Management raised its annual optical data center revenue outlook and emphasized strong customer bookings extending into 2028.

The discussion centered on the company's transition toward higher-speed interconnect technologies, growing hyperscaler engagement and supply constraints that could influence future revenue growth.

MXL Raises Optical Revenue Outlook on AI Demand

CEO Kishore Seendripu raised the company's 2026 optical data center revenue outlook to $250-$270 million, citing stronger demand for its PAM4 digital signal processor (DSP) products.

Infrastructure revenues increased 210% year over year to approximately $125 million, becoming MaxLinear's largest revenue category. The Keystone 800G platform remained the primary growth driver, supported by production deployments across multiple hyperscalers.

CFO Steven Litchfield said management expects optical DSP growth to exceed overall market growth in 2027, supported by customer demand and expanding market share.

MaxLinear Targets Higher Fourth-Quarter Revenues

For fourth-quarter 2026, management projected revenues of $240-$260 million, with infrastructure growth expected to offset seasonal weakness in broadband and connectivity.

Litchfield guided non-GAAP gross margin in the range of 59%-62% and operating expenses of $65-$70 million. Management expects infrastructure-heavy product mix to support margin improvement despite manufacturing cost pressures.

Third-quarter revenues reached $218.06 million, exceeding the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $215 million. Adjusted earnings of 62 cents per share surpassed the consensus estimate of 56 cents. Non-GAAP operating margin improved to 29.5% from 22.3% sequentially.

MaxLinear, Inc Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

MaxLinear, Inc price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | MaxLinear, Inc Quote

MXL Sees 1.6T Products Driving Future Expansion

Seendripu outlined accelerating qualification activity for Rushmore, the company's 200-gigabit-per-lane platform supporting 1.6T optical architectures.

During questioning from Stifel, he clarified that initial 1.6T shipments could begin in early 2027, followed by stronger second-half deployments. Management expects 2028 to represent a more substantial growth period.

Seendripu also indicated that DSP average selling prices are approximately doubling during the transition from 800G to 1.6T. Bundling Washington transimpedance amplifiers could increase content value further, with management targeting broader attachment rates.

MaxLinear Addresses Supply Constraints and Bookings

StoneX analysts questioned management about order visibility and capacity limitations. Litchfield indicated that customers are placing orders throughout 2027 and into 2028, despite optical product lead times of approximately 26-28 weeks.

During Susquehanna's questioning about potential overordering, Seendripu rejected concerns about double ordering, emphasizing disciplined customer procurement. He identified semiconductor foundry capacity as a more significant supply limitation.

Needham analysts also examined rising wafer prepayments. Litchfield expects further increases as demand expands, while the company increased its revolving credit facility by $70 million to $200 million to support additional capacity requirements.

MXL Expands Beyond Optical Connectivity

Management highlighted Annapurna electrical interconnects and Washington optical components as additional growth opportunities. Initial revenues are expected in 2027, followed by stronger adoption in 2028.

Seendripu also discussed RackCommander, which addresses telemetry, power management and control-plane connectivity within AI infrastructure. Panther storage acceleration and XGS-PON data center connectivity broaden the portfolio.

Meanwhile, broadband and connectivity revenues improved sequentially, supported by fiber deployments and Wi-Fi 7 gateways. Litchfield expects broadband growth in 2027 despite near-term seasonal softness.

MaxLinear Maintains Focus on Execution

Management's tone remained confident regarding AI infrastructure demand, customer qualifications and expanding product opportunities. However, foundry capacity constraints and qualification complexity remain important execution considerations.

Seendripu emphasized continued product diversification and deeper hyperscaler engagement, while Litchfield highlighted operating discipline and improved liquidity as priorities supporting anticipated growth.

What MXL's Zacks Rank and Style Scores Indicate

MXL currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), indicating a neutral near-term earnings estimate revision outlook. Its Growth Score of A and Momentum Score of B reflect favorable growth characteristics and price momentum. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.

However, its Value Score of F indicates comparatively weak valuation attractiveness, while its VGM Score of C signals a mixed overall profile. These scores complement the Zacks Rank rather than independently determining investment prospects. The stock's Zacks Rank could change as analysts revise earnings estimates following the latest quarterly results.

excerpt: Cintas (CTAS) reported earnings 30 days ago. What's next for the stock? We take a look at earnings estimates for some clues.
headline: Cintas (CTAS) Up 13.3% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Continue?
html_content:
It has been about a month since the last earnings report for Cintas (CTAS). Shares have added about 13.3% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500.

But investors have to be wondering, will the recent positive trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Cintas due for a pullback? Before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late, let's take a quick look at its latest earnings report in order to get a better handle on the important catalysts.

Cintas’ Q1 Earnings & Revenues Beat Estimates on Margin Gains

Cintas reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings of $1.39 per share, which beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.35 by 3.0%. The bottom line increased 15.8% from the year-ago quarter. Revenues of $3.01 billion surpassed the consensus estimate of $2.97 billion by 1.6% and rose 10.9% year over year.

The top line benefited from 8.9% organic revenue growth, reflecting growth after adjusting for acquisitions, foreign currency movements and workday differences. Record gross and operating margins were other key highlights in the quarter.

Cintas' Segmental Results

The company has two reportable segments, Uniform Rental and Facility Services and First Aid and Safety Services. Other businesses are included in All Other. Quarterly sales data are briefly discussed below.

Cintas' Uniform Rental and Facility Services segment generated revenues of $2.29 billion, up 9.7% year over year from $2.09 billion. Segment operating income rose to $575.09 million from $499.94 million.

The First Aid and Safety Services segment delivered revenues of $388.52 million, increasing 16.1% from $334.66 million in the prior-year quarter. Operating income climbed to $99.54 million from $80.33 million.

Revenues from the All Other segment totaled $330.73 million, up 13.1% from $292.40 million a year ago. Segment operating income increased to $51.67 million from $37.60 million.

Margin Profile

Cintas' cost of sales totaled $1.46 billion compared with $1.35 billion in the year-ago quarter. Gross margin increased 13.7% to $1.55 billion, while gross margin as a percentage of revenue expanded to 51.5% from 50.3%.

Selling and administrative expenses were $827.24 million, up 10.5% year over year. The company also incurred $14.41 million of transaction expenses related to the proposed UniFirst Corporation acquisition. Operating income rose 15.2% to $711.89 million.

Operating margin improved to 23.6% from 22.7% in the prior-year quarter. Net income increased 12.3% to $551.71 million, while net income margin was 18.3% compared with 18.1%. The effective tax rate increased to 20.0% from 17.6%.

Cintas' Cash Flow Trends

In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Cintas generated $572.33 million in net cash from operating activities, up from $414.48 million in the year-ago period. Capital expenditures totaled $107.53 million compared with $101.96 million a year earlier.

Free cash flow increased to $464.80 million from $312.52 million. Net cash used in investing activities was $117.37 million, reflecting capital expenditures, purchases of investments and business acquisitions.

During the quarter, the company repurchased common stock worth $315.71 million and paid $180.70 million in dividends. Net cash used in financing activities totaled $500.17 million.

Balance Sheet

Cintas exited the quarter with cash and cash equivalents of $243.60 million compared with $289.02 million at the end of fiscal 2026. Accounts receivable increased to $1.59 billion from $1.56 billion, while inventories declined to $433.29 million from $446.44 million.

Total current assets were $3.93 billion compared with $3.85 billion at May 31, 2026. Long-term debt was $1.43 billion, while debt due within one year totaled $999.29 million. Total shareholders' equity increased to $5.20 billion from $5.14 billion.

Cintas' Fiscal 2027 Outlook

For fiscal 2027, the company raised its revenue guidance to $12.15-$12.27 billion from the prior projection of $12.10-$12.25 billion. Adjusted diluted earnings per share are now projected in the range of $5.45-$5.54, up from $5.36-$5.50 previously.

The guidance excludes expected impacts from the proposed UniFirst acquisition and assumes no future acquisitions and constant foreign exchange rates. Fiscal 2027 also has one more workday than fiscal 2026.

Cintas expects net interest expense of approximately $103.00 million compared with $101.20 million in fiscal 2026, with the increase primarily tied to amortization of bridge loan financing expenses related to UniFirst. The company projects an effective tax rate of 20.4% for fiscal 2027.

How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?

Since the earnings release, investors have witnessed a upward trend in estimates revision.

VGM Scores

At this time, Cintas has a nice Growth Score of B, though it is lagging a bit on the Momentum Score front with a C. However, the stock has a score of F on the value side, putting it in the bottom 20% quintile for this investment strategy.

Overall, the stock has an aggregate VGM Score of D. If you aren't focused on one strategy, this score is the one you should be interested in.

Outlook

Estimates have been broadly trending upward for the stock, and the magnitude of these revisions looks promising. It comes with little surprise Cintas has a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). We expect an above average return from the stock in the next few months.

excerpt: Formula 1 weekends can cost a small fortune, but Meredith Margrave says the best money she spent at this year's race in Austin went to something far less glamorous: parking.
headline: I Splurged on Parking. It Changed the Way I Think About Money
html_content:
I'm writing this from Austin, Texas, where my husband and I are spending the weekend doing one of our favorite things: watching Formula 1 cars fly around the Circuit of the Americas at roughly 200 miles per hour.

If you've never been to a Formula 1 race, let me tell you something: It is expensive. Between the tickets, hotel, food, merchandise, and everything else that comes with a major sporting event, you can spend a small fortune before you've even seen a car.

And that's before you get into the upgrades. Once you've convinced yourself that spending an obscene amount of money to watch cars drive around a track is a reasonable vacation, spending a little more starts to seem like no big deal.

My husband and I have the same conversation every year. Should we spring for grandstand seats, or is general admission good enough? Do we really need tickets for all three days? What about the hospitality packages? (Just kidding about that last one. Some of those cost more than my first car.)

Over the years, we've landed on a few different answers. One year, we kept things simple and treated ourselves to grandstand seats for a day. Another year, we flipped the math and bought three-day general admission tickets so we could soak up the entire weekend at the track.

But last year, we decided to splurge on something completely new.

Parking.

Not paddock access. Not a hospitality lounge with complimentary champagne. A parking spot. And it might have been the best money we spent all weekend.

The Most Unexciting Luxury I've Ever Purchased

Circuit of the Americas is enormous, and when you're attending an event with hundreds of thousands of other people over a single weekend, getting from your car to the gate becomes an event of its own.

In previous years, we'd done what most reasonable people do. We'd paid about $40 to $60 a day to park in one of the sprawling lots surrounding the track. Then we'd walked. And walked. And walked some more. Depending on where we ended up, it could take close to an hour to reach the entrance.

On the way in, when you're excited and caffeinated, that walk doesn't seem like such a big deal. On the way out, after eight or ten hours of Texas heat, long lines, and steep hills, that hike back to the car feels like a personal attack. And once you finally reach the car, you get to join thousands of other exhausted people trying to leave the same lots at the same time. By the time we made it back to the hotel, the excitement of the day had been replaced by sore feet, traffic-induced irritation, and a desperate need for a shower.

So last year, we paid $400 for three days of garage parking by the main entrance.

And oh my.

Instead of spending the last hour of every day trudging across what felt like half of Central Texas, we walked a few hundred feet to our car. No dusty hike, no trying to remember which enormous field we'd parked in, and no ending an otherwise wonderful day by silently questioning every life choice that brought us there. We just got in the car and left. There wasn't even any post-event traffic. It was glorious.

When friends told us they were going to their first race this year and asked which upgrades were worth the money, my husband and I didn't even have to discuss it.

"Garage parking," we told them.

Sometimes the Best Splurge Is the One You Barely Notice

That decision illustrates something we tend to overlook when we talk about being smart with money.

We're very good at comparing prices. We can look at two hotel rooms, airline tickets, or concert seats and tell you which one costs less, down to the dollar. We're not always as good at comparing what we're actually getting for that money, especially the things that are hard to put a price tag on: our time, our energy, our patience, and our ability to enjoy something we've already paid a lot to experience.

Our garage parking didn't make the cars go any faster or give us a better view of the race. It didn't come with any perks we could brag about. What it did was eliminate the worst part of every day, and that turned out to be worth more to us than any of the fancier upgrades we'd considered.

That doesn't mean everyone should pay extra for parking. For some people, the walk is part of the adventure. Others would happily endure it to afford better seats. That's the point: What feels like a waste of money to one person can be a game-changer for another.

A nonstop flight might be worth every extra penny to someone who dreads connections. A hotel within walking distance of everything might be a better use of your vacation budget than a bigger room across town. And if you've ever traveled with young children, you already know that paying a little more to make something easier can be the difference between a family vacation and an elaborate exercise in suffering.

None of these things is glamorous. But money doesn't have to buy glamour to buy happiness. Sometimes it just buys you a little less aggravation.

Being Good With Money Doesn't Mean Being Cheap

Those of us who spend a lot of time thinking about personal finance tend to treat spending less as an accomplishment in itself. Sometimes it is! Finding a cheaper option that gives you the same experience is a win. So is skipping an upgrade you don't care about.

But the cheapest option isn't automatically the smartest one. What's the point of carefully saving for an experience if you won't spend a little more to make it genuinely enjoyable?

That doesn't mean throwing out the budget. If I let myself declare every little upgrade a "quality-of-life investment," we'd be in serious trouble. There still have to be trade-offs, and that's exactly why our parking decision felt so good. We didn't buy every upgrade, and we didn't decide that since we were already spending a lot, we might as well spend a lot more. We picked what mattered most to us.

Three days at the track? Absolutely. Premium seats? Nice, but we can live without them.

Not ending every day trudging through a parking lot like two survivors of a desert expedition?

Worth every penny.

So the next time you're planning a trip or a big purchase, don't just ask whether you can get it for less. Ask which part you're most likely to dread, and whether a little extra money would fix it. If it would, that might be a better use of your budget than the upgrade everyone else is buying.

The goal of managing your money isn't to spend as little of it as humanly possible. It's to make sure the money you do spend is doing something worthwhile for you.

This weekend, we're back at the track for another three days of racing, exploring, and spending entirely too much money on food. When the last car crosses the finish line on Sunday, thousands of people will begin the long journey back to their cars.

We'll walk a few hundred feet to ours.

Is that a luxury? Absolutely. Is it necessary? Not even a little. But if you'd asked me a few years ago whether parking would ever be a highlight of my vacation, I'd have laughed.

Now I wouldn't do it any other way.

excerpt: Stocks have faced a rough stretch lately, but Ethan Feller believes it may be setting up a year-end surge. Discover how the AI boom and deficit spending have created an environment that could propel the market higher as 2026 comes to a close.
headline: Positioned for a Rally: 5 Reasons Stocks Could Soar into Year-End
html_content:
The stock market has endured a difficult stretch these last few weeks, with the Nasdaq 100 suffering a sharp correction and selling pressure spreading across growth stocks and other economically sensitive areas.

But zooming out, the frustration has been building for months. Despite strong year-to-date returns, the major indexes have made relatively little sustained progress since early summer, as a growing list of concerns has weighed on investor sentiment.

Rising interest rates, persistent conflict in the Middle East, elevated oil prices, tighter Federal Reserve policy and renewed questions surrounding the sustainability of the AI boom have all contributed to an increasingly uncertain environment.

However, I believe the market may be approaching an important turning point.

For much of this bull market, I have argued that two powerful forces have been driving equities higher: the historic AI capital expenditure boom and persistent fiscal deficit spending. 

AI infrastructure investment is generating extraordinary revenue and earnings growth across semiconductors, memory, networking, power generation and a rapidly expanding ecosystem of related industries. Meanwhile, substantial government deficit spending continues to support nominal economic growth and corporate revenues, even as it creates longer-term fiscal challenges.

Neither of these underlying forces have disappeared. Rather, their positive influence has recently been overshadowed by a series of bearish macroeconomic developments.

And that is what makes the current setup particularly interesting.

With valuations improving, corporate earnings remaining exceptionally strong and several potential catalysts approaching, I believe the recent correction could prove to be the foundation for a powerful rally into year-end and early 2027.

Here are five reasons why. 

1) Stock Market Valuations Have Reset 

One of the most encouraging developments has been the improvement in equity valuations.

While stock prices have struggled in recent months, corporate earnings and forward estimates have continued climbing. That combination has produced meaningful valuation compression, particularly across the leading sectors.

This is an important distinction. A market doesn't necessarily need to experience a major bear market to become more attractively valued. Extended periods of sideways price action can accomplish much the same thing, provided earnings continue growing. And that is largely what has happened.

The Nasdaq-100, for example, now trades around 20 times forward earnings, compared with its 10-year median of approximately 23 times. That represents a notable discount to its historical valuation, despite the index's substantial exposure to some of the world's fastest growing and most profitable companies.

Of course, not everything is cheap. Some AI infrastructure businesses still command substantial premiums, and elevated Treasury yields make those valuations more difficult to justify. But the broader opportunity has clearly improved.

Many high-quality companies are now trading at substantially more reasonable multiples than they were earlier this year, even as analysts have continued raising earnings expectations.

Should interest rates stabilize and investor sentiment improve, those companies could benefit from both continued earnings growth and renewed valuation expansion. 

2) Corporate Earnings Are Booming and Could Broaden Significantly 

Perhaps the strongest argument for the bull market is the remarkable resilience of corporate earnings.

According to the latest Zacks estimates, S&P 500 earnings are expected to increase +24.6% year over year in the third quarter, supported by +11.8% revenue growth. That would mark the eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit earnings growth.

Those are extraordinary numbers, particularly considering the challenging macroeconomic backdrop. But an even more interesting story is unfolding beneath the surface.

The Magnificent Seven are expected to deliver earnings growth of +20.3%, supported by +22.9% revenue growth. However, excluding those seven companies, earnings growth for the rest of the S&P 500 actually increases to +26.0%.

That is a notable development, challenging the widely held assumption that only a handful of mega-cap technology stocks are supporting the market.

Much of that strength is coming from the broader AI infrastructure ecosystem, particularly semiconductor and memory manufacturers, alongside the energy sector. Technology sector earnings are expected to grow +43.3% in Q3, while Energy sector profits are projected to surge +118.1%.

For perspective, an earlier Zacks analysis showed that excluding both Technology and Energy, third-quarter earnings growth for the remaining S&P 500 companies was expected to be just +7.4%. 

The takeaway is that earnings growth remains exceptionally strong, but concentrated. And that concentration creates an important opportunity heading into 2027.

The next phase of this earnings cycle could feature substantially broader participation.

For the fourth quarter, S&P 500 earnings are projected to grow another +27.4%, supported by +12.3% revenue growth, with 15 of the 16 Zacks sectors expected to report positive earnings growth.

Looking further ahead, Zacks projects full-year S&P 500 earnings growth of +28.8% in 2026, followed by another +19.0% in 2027. Even excluding Technology, earnings are expected to increase +11.7% next year, while energy is expected to actually function as a drag on earnings next year.

More importantly, 15 of the 16 Zacks sectors are projected to grow earnings in 2027, with 11 expected to deliver double-digit gains.

The revisions trend is also encouraging. Since the beginning of July, analysts have raised their 2027 earnings estimates across 10 of the 16 Zacks sectors, with upward revisions extending beyond Technology into Finance, Industrials and other industries.

There is reason to believe that process could continue.

If energy prices retreat and interest rates stabilize, companies facing elevated transportation, financing and other operating costs could experience meaningful margin relief. That would support profitability across a much broader portion of the economy.

And importantly, this doesn't require the AI investment boom to end.

My preferred scenario is one in which AI infrastructure spending continues generating exceptional growth, while improving economic conditions allow more traditional industries to contribute meaningfully to the earnings expansion. 

That combination of sustained AI investment and broadening corporate profitability could provide the foundation for a much healthier, more broadly supported bull market in 2027.

3) One of the Market's Most Bullish Seasonal Windows Is Approaching 

The calendar is another reason I am becoming increasingly constructive.

Historically, the months leading up to midterm elections have been among the most challenging periods of the four-year presidential cycle for equity investors. Stocks have frequently experienced heightened volatility and meaningful corrections during this window, with the stretch from late summer through Election Day proving particularly difficult.

This year's market action has followed that historical pattern remarkably closely. Despite strong underlying corporate earnings, stocks have struggled to make sustained progress since early summer, with selling pressure intensifying as the November 3 midterm elections approach.

But what happens afterward is especially interesting. 

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months following every midterm election, a perfect 19-for-19 record.

Historical calculations show a median gain of approximately +14.5% over those subsequent 12 months.

The shorter-term record is also encouraging. Research from Schaeffer's Investment Research found that the S&P 500 gained an average of approximately +2.7% between Election Day and year-end during midterm election years, with positive returns about two-thirds of the time.

And the year following a midterm election has historically been the strongest year of the four-year presidential cycle.

There are several possible explanations.

For one, the election removes a major source of uncertainty. Investors can begin assessing actual policy outcomes rather than speculating about potential changes in taxes, regulation and government spending.

Political gridlock can also be viewed favorably, particularly when it reduces the likelihood of disruptive legislative changes.

Of course, historical patterns are not guarantees, and seasonality alone cannot overcome deteriorating earnings or a significant macroeconomic shock.

Nevertheless, the consistency of post-midterm strength is difficult to ignore.

With the election now approaching, the market is entering a period that has historically been exceptionally favorable for equities.

4) Oil and Interest Rates Could Become Powerful Tailwinds

Of all the factors weighing on stocks recently, rising oil prices and interest rates have arguably been the most consequential.

The ongoing conflict involving Iran has introduced a substantial geopolitical risk premium into global energy markets, pushing crude oil above $100 per barrel.

Higher energy costs create multiple problems for the economy. They increase transportation and manufacturing expenses, squeeze household purchasing power and contribute directly to inflation.

Perhaps most importantly for equity investors, higher inflation has complicated the Federal Reserve's policy outlook and contributed to rising Treasury yields.

The 10-year Treasury yield has recently traded above 5%, a level that creates meaningful competition for equities and raises financing costs throughout the economy.

But the relationship works in both directions.

If geopolitical tensions begin easing and oil prices retreat, several of these headwinds could reverse simultaneously.

Lower energy prices would relieve inflationary pressure, potentially allowing interest rate expectations to moderate. Consumers would benefit from lower gasoline prices, while transportation, manufacturing and other energy-intensive businesses could enjoy improving profit margins.

That combination could prove particularly favorable for small-cap stocks, cyclical industries and other market segments that have struggled under the weight of rising borrowing costs.

There is also a possible political catalyst approaching.

With the midterm elections nearly complete, the political incentives surrounding the Middle East conflict could begin changing, potentially creating an opening for renewed diplomatic efforts.

I would not base an investment strategy on predicting a geopolitical resolution. The conflict could just as easily intensify, keeping oil and rates elevated.

However, markets are already reflecting a substantial degree of concern about inflation and higher borrowing costs.

Even a modest improvement in those conditions could be enough to generate a meaningful shift in investor sentiment.

And if the AI spending boom and fiscal support remain intact, the removal of these macroeconomic headwinds could allow the market's underlying bullish forces to reassert themselves. 

5) A New Wave of AI IPOs Could Reignite Risk Appetite 

Finally, one of the more interesting potential catalysts is the approaching wave of major artificial intelligence initial public offerings.

For several years, investors have been able to participate in the AI boom primarily through established technology companies and the businesses supplying the infrastructure behind the industry.

But that could soon change. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, is reportedly preparing for a potential public offering, with speculation pointing toward a possible debut following the midterm elections. Meanwhile, OpenAI is pursuing additional financing and could eventually become another major entrant into the public markets.

These companies represent some of the most closely watched businesses in the world, and their potential listings could become important events for investor sentiment.

One of the largest uncertainties hanging over the AI investment boom is the underlying economics of the companies developing frontier AI models. Investors have relatively little visibility into their revenues, profitability, operating costs and long-term capital requirements. That uncertainty has raised legitimate questions about whether the enormous sums being invested in AI infrastructure will ultimately generate sufficient returns.

Public listings could go a long way toward resolving those concerns.

Greater financial transparency would allow investors to better assess the underlying business models, including revenue growth, margins, customer demand and the economics of developing and operating increasingly sophisticated AI systems.

And while the results could certainly disappoint, many of the recent indications surrounding enterprise adoption, revenue growth and demand for AI services have been encouraging. There is a reasonable possibility that greater transparency could reveal businesses with substantially stronger economics than skeptics currently assume.

That would have implications far beyond the companies themselves.

If investors gain confidence that frontier AI developers can build sustainable, profitable businesses, it would help validate the enormous infrastructure investments being made throughout the industry. That could relieve a major source of uncertainty weighing on semiconductor manufacturers, data center operators, power providers and other AI beneficiaries.

Of course, the opposite outcome is also possible. Disclosures revealing persistent losses, deteriorating unit economics or unsustainable capital requirements could reinforce concerns about an AI investment bubble.

Large IPOs also introduce additional equity supply, potentially absorbing capital that might otherwise flow into existing stocks.

Nevertheless, historically, active and successful IPO markets have tended to accompany periods of strong investor confidence and healthy risk appetite.

If these landmark AI offerings are well received, and the financial disclosures support the increasingly optimistic outlook for AI adoption, they could provide a powerful catalyst for renewed enthusiasm across the entire investment theme. 

What Could Go Wrong? 

Despite these encouraging developments, there are several risks that deserve attention.

The most immediate is the possibility that oil prices and Treasury yields continue climbing, forcing the Federal Reserve to maintain an even more restrictive policy stance.

A further escalation in the Middle East could intensify those pressures and weigh heavily on economic activity.

The other major risk is a meaningful deterioration in AI infrastructure spending.

Much of the market's earnings growth remains tied to enormous capital expenditure commitments from hyperscalers and other technology companies. A material reduction in those spending plans, or evidence that financing conditions are beginning to constrain investment, would directly challenge my underlying bull market thesis.

Finally, earnings expectations are already high. Even strong results may not be enough if corporate guidance begins deteriorating.

These are meaningful concerns, and the market could certainly experience further volatility before a durable advance takes hold. 

The Bull Market's Engines Are Still Running 

The recent market correction has been uncomfortable, but I don't believe the fundamental drivers of the bull market have disappeared.

AI infrastructure investment continues to support exceptional corporate earnings growth, while substantial fiscal deficit spending remains an important source of economic demand.

At the same time, valuations have improved, the earnings outlook remains strong, and the market is approaching one of its most historically favorable seasonal windows.

A potential decline in oil prices, stabilization in interest rates and renewed enthusiasm surrounding major AI IPOs could provide additional catalysts.

Not all five developments need to play out perfectly.

In fact, if even a few of these headwinds begin reversing while the underlying earnings expansion continues, the market could find itself in a substantially more favorable position heading into 2027.

Rather than signaling the end of the bull market, the recent pullback may ultimately prove to be the setup for its next major advance.

Our expert-led recommendation services highlight the most promising stocks on the market, including the hottest AI firms, insider trades (the legal kind), home run moves, stocks under $10, earnings surprise stocks, and more.

Looking further ahead, Zacks projects full-year S&P 500 earnings growth of +28.8% in 2026, followed by another +19.0% in 2027. Even excluding Technology, earnings are expected to increase +11.7% next year, while energy is expected to actually function as a drag on earnings next year. More importantly, 15 of the 16 Zacks sectors are projected to grow earnings in 2027, with 11 expected to deliver double-digit gains. The revisions trend is also encouraging. Since the beginning of July, analysts have raised their 2027 earnings estimates across 10 of the 16 Zacks sectors, with upward revisions extending beyond Technology into Finance, Industrials and other industries. There is reason to believe that process could continue. If energy prices retreat and interest rates stabilize, companies facing elevated transportation, financing and other operating costs could experience meaningful margin relief. That would support profitability across a much broader portion of the economy. And importantly, this doesn't require the AI investment boom to end. My preferred scenario is one in which AI infrastructure spending continues generating exceptional growth, while improving economic conditions allow more traditional industries to contribute meaningfully to the earnings expansion. That combination of sustained AI investment and broadening corporate profitability could provide the foundation for a much healthier, more broadly supported bull market in 2027. 3) One of the Market's Most Bullish Seasonal Windows Is Approaching The calendar is another reason I am becoming increasingly constructive. Historically, the months leading up to midterm elections have been among the most challenging periods of the four-year presidential cycle for equity investors. Stocks have frequently experienced heightened volatility and meaningful corrections during this window, with the stretch from late summer through Election Day proving particularly difficult. This year's market action has followed that historical pattern remarkably closely. Despite strong underlying corporate earnings, stocks have struggled to make sustained progress since early summer, with selling pressure intensifying as the November 3 midterm elections approach. But what happens afterward is especially interesting. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months following every midterm election, a perfect 19-for-19 record. Historical calculations show a median gain of approximately +14.5% over those subsequent 12 months. The shorter-term record is also encouraging. Research from Schaeffer's Investment Research found that the S&P 500 gained an average of approximately +2.7% between Election Day and year-end during midterm election years, with positive returns about two-thirds of the time. And the year following a midterm election has historically been the strongest year of the four-year presidential cycle. There are several possible explanations. For one, the election removes a major source of uncertainty. Investors can begin assessing actual policy outcomes rather than speculating about potential changes in taxes, regulation and government spending. Political gridlock can also be viewed favorably, particularly when it reduces the likelihood of disruptive legislative changes. Of course, historical patterns are not guarantees, and seasonality alone cannot overcome deteriorating earnings or a significant macroeconomic shock. Nevertheless, the consistency of post-midterm strength is difficult to ignore. With the election now approaching, the market is entering a period that has historically been exceptionally favorable for equities. 4) Oil and Interest Rates Could Become Powerful Tailwinds Of all the factors weighing on stocks recently, rising oil prices and interest rates have arguably been the most consequential. The ongoing conflict involving Iran has introduced a substantial geopolitical risk premium into global energy markets, pushing crude oil above $100 per barrel. Higher energy costs create multiple problems for the economy. They increase transportation and manufacturing expenses, squeeze household purchasing power and contribute directly to inflation. Perhaps most importantly for equity investors, higher inflation has complicated the Federal Reserve's policy outlook and contributed to rising Treasury yields. The 10-year Treasury yield has recently traded above 5%, a level that creates meaningful competition for equities and raises financing costs throughout the economy. But the relationship works in both directions. If geopolitical tensions begin easing and oil prices retreat, several of these headwinds could reverse simultaneously. Lower energy prices would relieve inflationary pressure, potentially allowing interest rate expectations to moderate. Consumers would benefit from lower gasoline prices, while transportation, manufacturing and other energy-intensive businesses could enjoy improving profit margins. That combination could prove particularly favorable for small-cap stocks, cyclical industries and other market segments that have struggled under the weight of rising borrowing costs. There is also a possible political catalyst approaching. With the midterm elections nearly complete, the political incentives surrounding the Middle East conflict could begin changing, potentially creating an opening for renewed diplomatic efforts. I would not base an investment strategy on predicting a geopolitical resolution. The conflict could just as easily intensify, keeping oil and rates elevated. However, markets are already reflecting a substantial degree of concern about inflation and higher borrowing costs. Even a modest improvement in those conditions could be enough to generate a meaningful shift in investor sentiment. And if the AI spending boom and fiscal support remain intact, the removal of these macroeconomic headwinds could allow the market's underlying bullish forces to reassert themselves. 5) A New Wave of AI IPOs Could Reignite Risk Appetite Finally, one of the more interesting potential catalysts is the approaching wave of major artificial intelligence initial public offerings. For several years, investors have been able to participate in the AI boom primarily through established technology companies and the businesses supplying the infrastructure behind the industry. But that could soon change. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, is reportedly preparing for a potential public offering, with speculation pointing toward a possible debut following the midterm elections. Meanwhile, OpenAI is pursuing additional financing and could eventually become another major entrant into the public markets. These companies represent some of the most closely watched businesses in the world, and their potential listings could become important events for investor sentiment. One of the largest uncertainties hanging over the AI investment boom is the underlying economics of the companies developing frontier AI models. Investors have relatively little visibility into their revenues, profitability, operating costs and long-term capital requirements. That uncertainty has raised legitimate questions about whether the enormous sums being invested in AI infrastructure will ultimately generate sufficient returns. Public listings could go a long way toward resolving those concerns. Greater financial transparency would allow investors to better assess the underlying business models, including revenue growth, margins, customer demand and the economics of developing and operating increasingly sophisticated AI systems. And while the results could certainly disappoint, many of the recent indications surrounding enterprise adoption, revenue growth and demand for AI services have been encouraging. There is a reasonable possibility that greater transparency could reveal businesses with substantially stronger economics than skeptics currently assume. That would have implications far beyond the companies themselves. If investors gain confidence that frontier AI developers can build sustainable, profitable businesses, it would help validate the enormous infrastructure investments being made throughout the industry. That could relieve a major source of uncertainty weighing on semiconductor manufacturers, data center operators, power providers and other AI beneficiaries. Of course, the opposite outcome is also possible. Disclosures revealing persistent losses, deteriorating unit economics or unsustainable capital requirements could reinforce concerns about an AI investment bubble. Large IPOs also introduce additional equity supply, potentially absorbing capital that might otherwise flow into existing stocks. Nevertheless, historically, active and successful IPO markets have tended to accompany periods of strong investor confidence and healthy risk appetite. If these landmark AI offerings are well received, and the financial disclosures support the increasingly optimistic outlook for AI adoption, they could provide a powerful catalyst for renewed enthusiasm across the entire investment theme. What Could Go Wrong? Despite these encouraging developments, there are several risks that deserve attention. The most immediate is the possibility that oil prices and Treasury yields continue climbing, forcing the Federal Reserve to maintain an even more restrictive policy stance. A further escalation in the Middle East could intensify those pressures and weigh heavily on economic activity. The other major risk is a meaningful deterioration in AI infrastructure spending. Much of the market's earnings growth remains tied to enormous capital expenditure commitments from hyperscalers and other technology companies. A material reduction in those spending plans, or evidence that financing conditions are beginning to constrain investment, would directly challenge my underlying bull market thesis. Finally, earnings expectations are already high. Even strong results may not be enough if corporate guidance begins deteriorating. These are meaningful concerns, and the market could certainly experience further volatility before a durable advance takes hold. The Bull Market's Engines Are Still Running The recent market correction has been uncomfortable, but I don't believe the fundamental drivers of the bull market have disappeared. AI infrastructure investment continues to support exceptional corporate earnings growth, while substantial fiscal deficit spending remains an important source of economic demand. At the same time, valuations have improved, the earnings outlook remains strong, and the market is approaching one of its most historically favorable seasonal windows. A potential decline in oil prices, stabilization in interest rates and renewed enthusiasm surrounding major AI IPOs could provide additional catalysts. Not all five developments need to play out perfectly. In fact, if even a few of these headwinds begin reversing while the underlying earnings expansion continues, the market could find itself in a substantially more favorable position heading into 2027. Rather than signaling the end of the bull market, the recent pullback may ultimately prove to be the setup for its next major advance. headline: 2 Small Cap Stocks for Your Short List
html_content:
• (0:45) - Should You Consider Investing Into Small Cap Stocks Right Now?
  • (4:30) - Top Stock Picks To Add To Your Watch List
  • (32:00) - Episode Roundup: CLST & NVEC
  • Podcast@Zacks.com

 

Welcome to Episode #504 of the Zacks Market Edge Podcast.

Every week, host and Zacks stock strategist, Tracey Ryniec, is joined by guests to discuss the hottest investing topics in stocks, bonds, and ETFs and how it impacts your life.

This week, Tracey was joined by Zacks Small Cap Analyst, Mark Zinski, to discuss what is going on with the small caps in 2026.

In the first half of the year, small caps outperformed the large caps for the first time in years. But as of Oct 2026, that has reversed.

Over the last 3 months, the Russell 2000 has fallen 5.6% while the S&P 500 is still in the green, up 2.8%.

A Small Cap Buying Opportunity?

Investors are abandoning the small caps as the Federal Reserve raises interest rates. Higher interest rates make it more expensive for small companies to borrow, which can slow growth.

But the weakness can create buying opportunities.

Mark brings his expertise in the small caps to the podcast with two small caps stocks to consider.

2 Small Cap Stocks for Your Short List

1. Catalyst Bancorp, Inc. (CLST)

Catalyst Bancorp is a small cap Louisiana bank with a market cap of $68.3 million. Founded in 1922 it has branches in South Central Louisiana.

In July 2026, Catalyst Bancorp acquired Lakeside Bancshares which has branches in Southwest Louisiana. This acquisition doubled its asset base.

Shares of Catalyst Bancorp are up 7.6% year-to-date. But it remains cheap. Bank analysts use price-to-book (P/B) ratios to determine a bank’s value. Investors should buy at a P/B ratio of 1.0 and sell at 2.0. Catalyst Bancorp has a P/B ratio of just 0.88.

Large data centers and SpaceX are going into Louisiana which should boost economic growth.

Should a Louisiana bank like Catalyst Bancorp be on your small cap short list?

2. NVE Corp. (NVEC)

NVE Corp. develops and sells devices using spintronics, a nanotechnology it helped pioneer. It has licensed their spintronic magnetoresistive random access memory technology, commonly known as MRAM. NVE Corp is a small cap with a market cap of $354 million.

Shares of NVE Corp. have fallen 33.3% in the last month on the AI and semiconductor sell-off. Yet it recently reported fiscal second quarter 2027 earnings and saw gross margins of 78%.

NVE Corp. also pays a quarterly dividend of $1.00 per share which is currently yielding 5.9%, thanks to the sinking of the stock.

Should a small cap technology company like NVE Corp be on your short list?

What Else Do You Need to Know About the Small Caps?

Tune into this week’s podcast to find out.

Zacks' Research Chief Names "Stock Most Likely to Double"

Our team of experts has just released the 5 stocks with the greatest probability of gaining +100% or more in the coming months. Of those 5, Director of Research Sheraz Mian highlights the one stock set to climb highest.

This innovative software-as-a-service firm upped its user base +22% year over year. That rate is increasing and margins are expanding as AI efficiencies take effect. Of course, all our elite picks aren't winners, but this one could far surpass earlier Zacks' Stocks Set to Double like D-Wave Quantum, which shot up +680.1%.

excerpt: How a Neutral rated stock turned into a big winner.
headline: SIF: Anatomy of the One That Got Away
html_content:
Unfortunately, we sometimes miss some real winners. However, an autopsy of missed alpha can be instructive and help us refine our stock rating process and potentially challenge our team to acknowledge selection bias when appropriate.

Individual investors may have different risk tolerances and industry knowledge which essentially could override our rating decision. Our goal is to provide comprehensive and balanced research replete with information and opinions that enable informed investment decisions.

Additionally, no stock screener is fool proof, but it still provides value as a “first cut” process for sorting out potential winners. Even with the advances in AI, which have accelerated the stock research process and provide detailed pros and cons, stock picking will still ultimately rely upon some human judgement call for those who subscribe to active vs. passive investing.

We felt it worthwhile to evaluate a rich example of a missed opportunity, in this case, SIFCO Industries, Inc. (SIF).


Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

We launched coverage in February of 2025 with a Neutral rating. The stock was trading at about $3.60/share. SIFCO Industries, Inc. (SIF) provides forging and machine components primarily to the aerospace and defense industries. Exposure to the highly cyclical aerospace industry probably raised our risk antennae. And defense industry orders can be lumpy due to the procurement process.

Timing the turn-around and picking the bottom in a historically cyclical industry is inherently difficult, in my opinion. But what did the data suggest?

The latest quarter, Q4 of 2024, which ended 9/30/24, was improved with EPS loss narrowing to ($.33) vs ($.53) in the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA had also turned positive at $.8 m vs. ($1.5 m) in the prior year.
Q4 sales increased 14% YOY and backlog increased 17% YOY as well. 

Although management did not issue formal guidance for FY25, it did mention it was preparing to increase production based on customer demand.

The valuation at the time was reasonable, trading at about a 30% discount to Book Value and slightly less to Tangible Book Value. However, the business was still unprofitable, suggesting book value could continue declining, albeit at a lower rate.

The 5-year valuation analysis suggested the stock had traded as low as a 70% discount to Book Value so more downside was possible.

While Gross margin was improved at 7.5%, that was still relatively low, especially on a Marx ratio level (Gross Profit/Total Assets), so the stock was screening near the bottom of the microcap universe.

While debt had been materially reduced due to the divestiture, the rate on the revolver had increased to 9.8% vs. 8% and operating cash flow was barely positive for the FY, so interest rate exposure was an additional risk factor if the company was forced to draw on the revolver.

The company remained unprofitable, although less negative, for the next 2 quarters accompanied by backlog growth and some sales growth. However, the Gross Margin remained subdued at sub 6% so material leverage was still absent. Additionally, our ranking system was flashing Underperform because of the low Gross Margin. 

So, we remained on the sidelines. It appeared our initial assessment was prudent.

But then the calendar June 25 quarter came along, and the company generated EPS of $.54 vs. a loss of ($.16) in the prior year, benefiting from a one-time ERC (Employee Retention Credit) of $2.4 m which positively impacted Gross Margin, raising it to nearly 27%. Absent the credit, Gross Margin would have been about 15.8%.

But sales were flat for the quarter, casting doubt on cyclical recovery while potential exposure to new 50% tariffs on aluminum and steel loomed. Additionally, the cash balance remained relatively low at $1.9 m and interest rate exposure on the revolver remained a concern. Hence, we remained on the sidelines, but the stock essentially doubled to $7 on the suggested profitability turn-around.

I heard echoes of when back in the day I would occasionally run into an IR person at an investor conference and they would say, “Our stock is now at $7. Where were you at $3.50 when I introduced you to the name?” 

The stock maintained support around $7 for the next 2 quarters and valuation consequently rerated to about 1.2x Book value. Tariff impacts still loomed and we remained unconvinced regarding the durability of structural gross margin improvement. The strength of the aerospace and defense vertical recovery were also concerns.

But then the company reported calendar quarter ending 12/31/25 and the stock quickly doubled again to around $14. In that FY-Q1 sales grew 14.8% while backlog also increased YOY by 14%. But perhaps most importantly, Gross Margin improved YOY to 21.6% vs. 4.4% enabling EPS to grow to $.29 vs a loss of ($.40) in the prior year. Gross margin increased due to higher throughput, favorable pricing and mix shifts from exiting lower-margin work.

By now the stock had re-rated to 2.3x BV. So, we missed it. And the stock was trading at 5-year valuation highs so we just couldn’t pull the trigger, though the stock would double once again to $28+ before pulling back more recently.

This stock was very reminiscent of another microcap, Perma-Pipe International Holdings, Inc. (PPIH), which we’ve highlighted in previous articles. Similarly the company was exposed to cyclical and lumpy markets while trading at an attractive discount to Book Value.


Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

In the case of Perma-Pipe International Holdings, Inc. (PPIH), however, we felt more comfortable with the topline catalysts. And the business was profitable. That Outperform worked well after we launched coverage in May of 2024.

The point of this exercise is multi-fold. Firstly, we wanted to demonstrate more specifically our thought process as we monitor stocks after initiation. A constant process of weighing multiple factors is at play. Secondly, as we’ve written about previously, microcaps as an asset class are very volatile, on the magnitude of about 2x vs. large caps. And hence, valuations can re-rate significantly in quick order.

One could argue that perhaps we were too risk averse by fixating too much on Gross Margin, ignoring a possible margin of safety with the backlog increase and the attractive discount to tangible book value. 

But perhaps the most valuable lesson is that investors should not easily dismiss Neutral rated stocks, they too can produce significant alpha and are worth studying.

 

Zacks' Research Chief Names "Stock Most Likely to Double"

Our team of experts has just released the 5 stocks with the greatest probability of gaining +100% or more in the coming months. Of those 5, Director of Research Sheraz Mian highlights the one stock set to climb highest.

Of course, all our elite picks aren't winners, but this one could far surpass earlier Zacks' Stocks Set to Double like D-Wave Quantum, which shot up +680.1%.

headline: Bull of the Day: Hasbro (HAS)
html_content:
Hasbro HAS is a leading games, IP, and toy company with over 160 years of expertise. It reaches over 500 million kids, families, and fans around the world through physical and digital games, video games, toys, licensed consumer products, location-based entertainment, film, TV, and more.

The stock sports a favorable Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), with EPS revisions on a bullish trajectory across the board.

excerpt: Sector ETF report for XLE
headline: Should You Invest in the State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE)?
html_content:
The State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) was launched on December 16, 1998, and is a passively managed exchange traded fund designed to offer broad exposure to the Energy - Broad segment of the equity market.

While an excellent vehicle for long term investors, passively managed ETFs are a popular choice among institutional and retail investors due to their low costs, transparency, flexibility, and tax efficiency.

Additionally, sector ETFs offer convenient ways to gain low risk and diversified exposure to a broad group of companies in particular sectors. Energy - Broad is one of the 16 broad Zacks sectors within the Zacks Industry classification. It is currently ranked 2, placing it in top 13%.

Index Details

The fund is sponsored by State Street Investment Management. It has amassed assets over $46.1 billion, making it the largest ETF attempting to match the performance of the Energy - Broad segment of the equity market. XLE seeks to match the performance of the Energy Select Sector Index before fees and expenses.

The Energy Select Sector Index includes companies from the following industries: oil, gas & consumable fuels and energy equipment & services.

Costs

Since cheaper funds tend to produce better results than more expensive funds, assuming all other factors remain equal, it is important for investors to pay attention to an ETF's expense ratio.

Annual operating expenses for this ETF are 0.08%, making it the least expensive product in the space.

It has a 12-month trailing dividend yield of 2.2%.

Sector Exposure and Top Holdings

Even though ETFs offer diversified exposure that minimizes single stock risk, investors should also look at the actual holdings inside the fund. Luckily, most ETFs are very transparent products that disclose their holdings on a daily basis.

This ETF has heaviest allocation in the Energy sector -- about 100% of the portfolio.

Looking at individual holdings, Exxonmobil Holdings Corp (XOM) accounts for about 23.53% of total assets, followed by Chevron Corp (CVX) and Conocophillips (COP).

The top 10 holdings account for about 78.08% of total assets under management.

Performance and Risk

So far this year, XLE has added about 57.64%, and it's up approximately 59.27% in the last one year (as of 10/26/2026). During this past 52-week period, the fund has traded between $43.595 and $69.33.

The ETF has a beta of 0.48 and standard deviation of 21.37% for the trailing three-year period, making it a high risk choice in the space. With about 24 holdings, it has more concentrated exposure than peers.

Alternatives

State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF holds a Zacks ETF Rank of 1 (Strong Buy), which is based on expected asset class return, expense ratio, and momentum, among other factors. Because of this, XLE is a great option for investors seeking exposure to the Energy ETFs segment of the market. There are other additional ETFs in the space that investors could consider as well.

iShares Global Energy ETF (IXC) tracks S&P Global 1200 Energy Sector Index and the Vanguard Energy Index Fund ETF Shares (VDE) tracks MSCI US Investable Market Energy 25/50 Index. iShares Global Energy ETF has $3.43 billion in assets, Vanguard Energy Index Fund ETF Shares has $11.64 billion. IXC has an expense ratio of 0.37%, and VDE charges 0.09%.

Bottom Line

excerpt: Software ETFs surged last week as investors rotated away from AI infrastructure spending. Explore the key drivers and ETFs poised to benefit from the rally.
headline: Software ETFs: Hidden Gems Amid the AI Selloff?
html_content:
U.S. software stocks surged last week, erasing fears of a broad-based tech sector selloff. State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF XLK fell 1.8% last week against State Street SPDR S&P Software & Services ETF’s XSW 9% gain. The rally in XSW came in despite the fact that the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to around 5%.

Why Software Stocks Soared

The rally mainly happened because investors rotated out of the crowded, capital-heavy AI-infrastructure trade and back into beaten-down enterprise software—especially cybersecurity—while earnings and buybacks reinforced the value case.

According to a report by Bloomberg, the S&P 500 Software Index has just recorded its strongest weekly performance since May, as reported by Economic Times.

Investors have also been reassessing technology valuations amid rising rates and heavy corporate borrowing. With software stocks apparently less capital-heavy and less debt-laden, the segment is less exposed to rising rates.

Key Drivers

Rotation Away from AI-Capex Anxiety

Meta’s plan to raise capital for its AI buildout intensified concerns about how hyperscalers will finance enormous data-center spending. Investors sold AI-infrastructure-linked names and bought assets perceived as less dependent on that funding cycle, including software.

NVIDIA-backed neocloud major CoreWeave CRWV and bonds slumped ???lately on investor worries over debt financing. CRWV shares have lost 40% over the past month (read: Are Concerns Over CoreWeave's Debt Overblown? ETFs in Focus).

Cybersecurity Emerges Winner

A global alert over cyber threats caused by rogue AI agents triggered a security scramble, lifting Okta, Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike, and Cloudflare.  AI safety concerns and rising cyber threats are creating new tailwinds for the cybersecurity sector. Okta surged 12% last week, Palo Alto added 7.2%, CrowdStrike jumped 12% and Cloudflare rose 6.8%.

Attractive Valuation

Software was hit hard by AI-disruption fears, creating a bargain-hunting setup. Strong earnings expectations—roughly 27% projected earnings growth for Internet - Software firms —and large buyback announcements from companies such as Salesforce and Wix helped restore confidence. Per Economic Times, lower valuations led Salesforce and Wix to binge on buybacks.

The Zacks categorized Internet – Software industry currently trades at a forward price/earnings ratio of 20.75X versus the S&P 500’s 18.63X. Price/sales ratio of the industry (at 3.23X) is also in line with the S&P 500 (3.10X). The industry trades at a price/book ratio of 3.28X versus the S&P 500’s score of 3.66X, which makes the industry cheaper than the S&P 500.

Bottom Line

Valuation reset, earnings resilience, buybacks and AI monetization showed that the future ahead of software stocks is anything but dark. Meanwhile, cybersecurity stocks are serving to the AI-led attack complexity. Cybersecurity can be tagged as a relatively defensive play in the tech bunch.

ETFs in Focus

Against this backdrop, below we highlight a few software ETFs like iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) and XSW. The group also has some pure-play cybersecurity ETFs like Amplify Cybersecurity ETF HACK and First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF CIBR. IGV has added about 5.2% last week. HACK was up 1% while CIBR surged about 6%.

headline: 3 Top-Ranked BlackRock Mutual Funds With Strong Return Potential
html_content:
BlackRock Inc. is one of the world’s leading asset management firms offering a range of risk management, strategic advisory and enterprise investment system services. With about $15.3 trillion worth of assets under management (excluding money market assets) as of June 30, 2026, it caters to institutional, intermediary and individual investors.

Its offerings range from individual and institutional separate accounts to mutual funds and other pooled investment options. BlackRock aims to provide a wide range of investment solutions to strike a balance between risk and opportunities.

Below, we share with you three top-ranked BlackRock mutual funds, viz., BlackRock Advantage Large Cap Growth Fund BMCRX, BlackRock Impact U.S. Equity Fund BIRCX and BlackRock Tactical Opportunities Fund - Service PCBAX. Each has a Zacks Mutual Fund Rank #1 (Strong Buy) and is expected to outperform its peers in the future. Investors can click here to see the complete list of BlackRock mutual funds.

BlackRock Advantage Large Cap Growth Fund invests most of its assets, along with borrowings, if any, in common stocks, preferred stocks and derivative instruments that have similar economic characteristics. BMCRX advisors prefer to invest in large-cap growth companies that have characteristics similar to the securities listed in the Growth Indices.

BlackRock Advantage Large Cap Growth Fund has three-year annualized returns of 27.5%. As of the end of May 2026, BMCRX held 157 issues, with 9.2% of its net assets invested in NVIDIA Corp.

BlackRock Impact U.S. Equity Fund invests most of its assets, along with borrowings, if any, in large-cap equity securities. BIRCX advisors also invest in derivative issues with similar economic characteristics.

BlackRock Impact U.S. Equity Fund has three-year annualized returns of 22.7%. BIRCX has an expense ratio of 1.48%

BlackRock Tactical Opportunities Fund - Service invests most of its assets using a macro asset allocation strategy, in varying percentages in a portfolio of global stocks, bonds, money market instruments, foreign currencies and cash. PCBAX advisors also invest in common stocks, preferred stocks, convertible and non-convertible securities and depositary receipts.

BlackRock Tactical Opportunities Fund - Service has three-year annualized returns of 10%. Philip J. Green has been one of the fund managers of PCBAX since the end of December 2006.

To view the Zacks Rank and the past performance of all BlackRock mutual funds, investors can click here to see the complete list of BlackRock mutual funds.

excerpt: LMT shares jump 9.6% after a Q3 earnings beat and record backlog, putting defense ETFs with significant LMT exposure in focus.
headline: ETFs to Buy as Lockheed Shares Jump Post Q3 Earnings Beat, Record Backlog
html_content:
Shares of Lockheed Martin LMT have gained 9.6% following the defense giant’s better-than-expected third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 22. The rally was driven by revenue and earnings beats, along with a record backlog count, which reached an all-time high of $292 billion. 

The backlog was boosted by a massive $52.5 billion multi-year award for PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors, reflecting surging global demand for missile defense systems. The company’s raised full-year forecast likely further bolstered investor sentiment, contributing to the stock’s climb. 

However, the company’s cash flow situation presented a nuanced picture. Lockheed generated $3 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, representing a 9% decline from the prior-year period’s level. As the company remains in negotiations with the U.S. government over production contracts for F-35 Lots 20 and higher, Lockheed’s future cash flow may suffer a decline if additional funding is not received.

Against this backdrop, investors might want to consider exchange-traded funds (ETFs) with substantial exposure to Lockheed Martin as an alternative to investing directly in the stock. 

These ETFs will offer an opportunity to benefit from a potential rally in LMT stock, driven by geopolitical tensions and a seemingly insatiable demand for munitions and air defense, while avoiding the idiosyncratic risk and sharp volatility associated with a single-stock position.

Before exploring the best ETF options for gaining exposure to Lockheed Martin, let us take a closer look at the company’s third-quarter performance across key operational metrics and assess how the market, particularly credit rating agencies, responded to its results.

A Look at LMT’s Q3 Earnings

The company’s third-quarter earnings of $7.97 beat the Zacks consensus estimate by 6.4%, while its sales of $20.7 billion topped the consensus mark by 1.4%. On a year-over-year basis, both revenues and earnings recorded double-digit growth.  

The sales growth was driven by higher volume across every segment, including F-35 production and sustainment at Aeronautics, MFC munitions production ramps, new radar awards at the RMS unit, and growth in Fleet Ballistic Missile and Next-Generation Interceptor at the Space segment. 

Its backlog increased $113 billion compared with the prior-year period’s level.

LMT has raised its 2026 sales guidance to $80-$82 billion, the midpoint of which reflects year-over-year growth of 8%, but stands lower than the consensus estimate of $81.07 billion. The year-over-year increase in the top line is expected to be driven by higher volume in LMT’s

MFC unit as a result of munition ramp-ups and continued strength across the company’s portfolio as a whole. 

Lockheed Martin's space team has recently completed a key solid rocket motor test for the next-generation interceptor program, keeping that program on track for fielding by 2030 while strengthening homeland missile defense and advancing a capability considered essential to the nation's future (as reported by LMT on its third-quarter conference call). 

Moreover, the recent expansion of its Grand Prairie, TX, manufacturing footprint to more than 735,000 square feet includes additional capability and capacity for automation and digital manufacturing. This facility will also bring on board a Hadrian highly automated production machine cell to supply components across its missile programs under a manufacturing-as-a-service contract.

Such initiatives should continue to boost LMT’s position in the defense industry, offering solid growth potential. 

However, Lockheed’s rising capital expenditure, which rose 15.2%, remains a cause of concern for investors as it continues to squeeze the company's free cash flow (FCF) in the near term. 

Market Reaction

Following LMT’s third-quarter 2026 results, RBC Capital raised its price target on Lockheed Martin to $600 from $550 while maintaining a 'Sector Perform' rating, citing strong bookings and encouraging initial commentary on 2027. Citi analyst John Godyn also raised his price target for LMT to $706 from $691 and maintained a 'Buy' rating (as seen on Yahoo Finance).  

Lockheed-Heavy ETFs to Buy

Given these developments, the following ETFs could appeal to investors seeking to capitalize on Lockheed Martin’s growth potential while mitigating the risks associated with investing in a single stock:

Invesco Aerospace & Defense ETF PPA

This fund, with a market value of $7.28 billion, includes 68 companies involved in the development, manufacture, operation, and support of U.S. defense, military, national/homeland security and government space operations. LMT enjoys the first spot in this fund, holding 9.54% of its assets. 

PPA charges 58 basis points (bps) in fees and traded at a volume of 0.22 million shares in the last trading session. 

Global X Defense Tech ETF SHLD

This fund, with net assets worth $6.45 billion, offers exposure to 50 companies that build and manage cybersecurity systems, utilize artificial intelligence and big data, and build advanced military systems and hardware such as robotics, fuel systems, and aircrafts for defense applications. LMT enjoys the second spot in this fund, holding 9.51% of its assets. 

SHLD charges 50 bps in fees and traded at a volume of 0.72 million shares in the last trading session. 

U.S. Defense ETF DUTY

This fund, with net asset value of $27.87, includes 52 companies positioned to benefit from increased spending on traditional and modern defense technologies. LMT enjoys the second spot in this fund, holding 8.35% of its assets. 

DUTY charges 45 bps in fees and traded at a volume of 0.001 million shares in the last trading session. 

iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF ITA

This fund, with net assets worth $11.78 billion, offers exposure to 50 domestic aerospace and defense companies, including manufacturers of commercial and military aircraft. LMT enjoys the fourth spot in this fund, holding 5.59% of its assets. 

ITA charges 37 bps in fees and traded at a volume of 0.85 million shares in the last trading session.

headline: Implied Volatility Surging for PDF Solutions Stock Options
html_content:
Investors in PDF Solutions, Inc. PDFS need to pay close attention to the stock based on moves in the options market lately. That is because the Nov. 20, 2026 $22.50 Put had some of the highest implied volatility of all equity options today.

What is Implied Volatility?

Implied volatility shows how much movement the market is expecting in the future. Options with high levels of implied volatility suggest that investors in the underlying stocks are expecting a big move in one direction or the other. It could also mean there is an event coming up soon that may cause a big rally or a huge sell-off. However, implied volatility is only one piece of the puzzle when putting together an options trading strategy.

What do the Analysts Think?

Clearly, options traders are pricing in a big move for PDF Solutions shares, but what is the fundamental picture for the company? Currently, PDF Solutions is a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) in the Computer - Services industry that ranks in the Top 41% of our Zacks Industry Rank. Over the last 60 days, our Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current quarter has moved from 39 cents per share to 40 cents in that period.

Given the way analysts feel about PDF Solutions right now, this huge implied volatility could mean there’s a trade developing. Oftentimes, options traders look for options with high levels of implied volatility to sell premium. This is a strategy many seasoned traders use because it captures decay. At expiration, the hope for these traders is that the underlying stock does not move as much as originally expected.
